_comment: Cambridge 0097's Thinking and Working Scientifically and Science in Context objectives for Stage 2 that no Grade 2 unit reached, authored as reasoning prompts. Added 2026-09-17 with the Stages 1-4 re-point. FOUR prompts, not seven: three of the seven unclaimed Stage 2 TWS objectives turned out to be taught already and were claimed instead of authored - 2TWSa.03 and 2TWSc.06 by Unit 1, whose minibeast hunt and weather station have the learner tally into a table and then draw and read a bar chart, and 2TWSc.02 by Unit 5, which hands the learner a battery, wires and a bulb and has them build a circuit. Reading the content before writing new content is the cheaper half of closing a coverage gap and it is the half that gets skipped.
_vehicle: reasoningPrompts. See cambridge-stage1-enquiry.json for the full note on the deck-only section at Stages 1-4 and why appending is safe.
source: Authored 2026-09-17 against Cambridge 0097 Stage 2, anchored to the investigations in Grade 2 units 1-6.
_minimumCovered: One prompt per Stage 2 TWS/SIC objective that no unit's own content already delivers. Coverage is a number that only goes up.

prompts.prompt: You built a weather station and recorded the sky for a week. Name two people whose job needs weather records, and say what each of them would do with yours.
keyIdeas: A farmer plans planting around the rain
A pilot or a fisherman needs to know about wind
prompts.modelAnswer: A farmer would use the records to decide when to plant, because a seed sown just before the rains does best. A weather forecaster collects records from many places and warns people when a flood or a dust storm is coming. A fisherman checks the wind before going out. They all do what you did - collect data and read it - except it is their job.

prompts.prompt: You want to record how big each of your three rocks is, and you have no ruler and no scales. How could you measure their size and their weight using only things in the house?
keyIdeas: Line up paper clips or beans to measure length
Balance the rock against counted stones or spoons of sand
Use the same counting thing for every rock
prompts.modelAnswer: For size I can lay paper clips along the longest part of each rock and count them. For weight I can balance the rock on one side of a ruler over a pencil and count how many spoons of sand it takes on the other side. The important rule is to use the SAME paper clips and the same spoon for all three rocks, or I cannot compare the numbers.

prompts.prompt: Here are two ways of showing your circuit: a photograph of it on the table, and a drawing with a line for each wire and a simple sign for the battery and the bulb. What can the drawing do that the photograph cannot?
keyIdeas: A picture shows what it looks like
A diagram shows only the parts that matter
A diagram leaves out the colours, the table and the shadows
prompts.modelAnswer: The photograph shows what the circuit looks like - the colour of the wires, the table underneath, the shadow. The drawing is a diagram: it leaves all that out and keeps only the parts that matter, so you can see the loop clearly and follow the path all the way round. A picture shows how something looks; a diagram shows how something works.

prompts.prompt: You want to know what time the Sun will set next month, but you cannot wait a month to find out. Where could you look it up, and why is looking it up a fair way to answer a science question?
keyIdeas: A calendar, an almanac, a prayer timetable or a weather page
Somebody else has already watched and recorded it
You still check it against what you see
prompts.modelAnswer: I can look it up on a calendar, a prayer timetable or a weather page, because people have already watched the Sun for years and written the times down. Using what someone else carefully recorded is a real way of answering a science question, as long as I trust where it came from - and I can still check tomorrow's time against the sky myself.
